Empathy means trying to understand how someone else is feeling.
Including others in games helps everyone feel like they belong.
Taking slow, deep breaths can help your body calm down.
A growth mindset means believing you can improve with practice.
It takes courage to stand up for someone who is being bullied.
Saying thank you shows people that you appreciate them.

Good friends listen, share and support each other.
Disappointment is a normal feeling when things don't go to plan.
Writing in a journal can help you understand your feelings.
Being kind to yourself is just as important as being kind to others.

p: Everyone has feelings, and all feelings are okay. Sometimes we feel happy and excited, and sometimes we feel sad, angry or worried. What matters is how we respond. Talking to someone we trust, taking deep breaths or going for a walk can help us manage big feelings.

Empathy is the ability to imagine how someone else might be feeling. If a classmate looks upset, you might think about how you would feel in their situation. Then you can ask if they are okay or offer to help. Showing empathy helps build strong friendships and a kinder community.

A growth mindset is the belief that your abilities can grow with effort and practice. Instead of saying I can't do this, you can say I can't do this yet. People with a growth mindset see mistakes as chances to learn. This helps them keep trying when things get difficult.

Bullying is when someone keeps hurting another person on purpose, with words, actions or online messages. If you see bullying, you can be an upstander. You might tell the person to stop, help the person being bullied get away or tell a teacher. Doing nothing can make the bullying continue.

Our class keeps a gratitude jar. Every Friday, we each write one thing we are thankful for on a small piece of paper. Some people write about their families, some about their pets and some about a good day at school. Reading the notes at the end of the term always makes us smile.

When I feel nervous before a test, I use a strategy called box breathing. I breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold for four again. After a few rounds, my heart slows down and I can think more clearly.

s: Emotional intelligence involves recognising, understanding and managing your own feelings and those of others.
Resilience is not about avoiding difficulties but learning to recover and grow from them.
Peer pressure can be positive or negative depending on the choices it encourages.
Mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment without judging it.
Healthy relationships are built on respect, trust, honesty and good communication.
Comparing yourself to edited images on social media can harm your self-esteem.
Setting boundaries is a healthy way to protect your time, energy and wellbeing.
Anxiety is a common experience, and effective support is available for those who need it.
Active listening involves giving full attention, asking questions and reflecting back what you hear.
Volunteering can increase happiness by creating a sense of purpose and connection.
Conflict is a normal part of relationships and can be resolved respectfully.
Recognising early warning signs of stress helps you take action before it becomes overwhelming.
Inclusion means making sure everyone feels valued, regardless of their background or abilities.
Apologising sincerely involves acknowledging the hurt you caused and committing to change.
Sleep, nutrition and exercise all play a role in emotional wellbeing.
Gratitude practices have been linked to improved mood and stronger relationships.
Being an upstander means taking safe action when you see someone being treated unfairly.
Grief can show up in many ways, including sadness, anger, numbness and tiredness.
Self-compassion means treating yourself with the same kindness you would offer a friend.
Online friendships can be meaningful, but it is important to stay safe and protect your privacy.
Helplines such as Kids Helpline offer free and confidential support at any time.
Assertive communication expresses your needs clearly while respecting other people.
Celebrating small achievements can build motivation and confidence.
Loneliness affects people of all ages, and reaching out can make a real difference.
Kindness is contagious, encouraging others to pass it on.
p: Resilience is the ability to cope with challenges and bounce back from setbacks. It does not mean never feeling upset or stressed. Instead, resilient people use strategies such as problem-solving, seeking support and focusing on what they can control. Resilience can be developed over time, especially when young people have caring relationships and opportunities to practise coping skills.

Social media can help teenagers stay connected, explore interests and express creativity. However, it can also lead to comparison, cyberbullying and pressure to appear perfect. Many images online are edited or carefully selected, which can make others feel inadequate. Taking regular breaks, following accounts that make you feel good and remembering that online life is only a small part of reality can help.

Assertive communication is a skill that helps people express their thoughts and needs honestly while respecting others. It sits between being passive, where you stay silent, and being aggressive, where you ignore others' feelings. Using I statements, such as I feel frustrated when I am interrupted, can help explain your perspective without blaming. Assertiveness can improve relationships and reduce conflict.

Mindfulness is the practice of paying attention to the present moment. It might involve focusing on your breathing, noticing the sounds around you or observing your thoughts without reacting to them. Research suggests that regular mindfulness practice can reduce stress, improve concentration and help people respond to difficult emotions more calmly. Even a few minutes a day can be helpful.

Being an upstander means taking action when someone is being treated unfairly. This does not always mean confronting the person causing harm, which may not be safe. Upstanders might check in privately with the person affected, refuse to share hurtful content online or report the behaviour to a trusted adult. Small actions like these show that bullying is not acceptable.

Everyone experiences grief at some point, whether through the death of a loved one, the end of a friendship or a big change such as moving away. Grief can bring a mix of emotions and may come and go in waves. There is no right way to grieve. Talking about memories, keeping routines and seeking support from family, friends or counsellors can help.

s: Psychological research suggests that strong social connections are among the most reliable predictors of long-term wellbeing.
Emotional regulation involves noticing feelings, understanding their causes and choosing how to respond.
Stigma surrounding mental illness can prevent people from seeking help until problems become severe.
Empathy can be cultivated through reading, listening and deliberately engaging with different perspectives.
Perfectionism is often mistaken for high standards but can be driven by fear of failure and criticism.
Compassion fatigue can affect people who constantly care for others without attending to their own needs.
Cognitive behavioural strategies teach people to identify and challenge unhelpful patterns of thinking.
Kindness has measurable benefits, both for those who receive it and for those who offer it.
Healthy relationships require mutual respect, clear consent and the freedom to express disagreement.
Loneliness has been described as a public health concern because of its effects on physical and mental health.
Vulnerability, though uncomfortable, is often essential for forming genuine and lasting connections.
The transition to adulthood involves forming an independent identity while maintaining supportive relationships.
Coping strategies that provide short-term relief, such as avoidance, can sometimes worsen problems over time.
Restorative practices focus on repairing harm and rebuilding relationships rather than simply punishing wrongdoing.
Gratitude shifts attention towards what is present and valued, which can buffer against stress.
Discrimination has documented effects on mental health, highlighting the importance of inclusive communities.
Meaning and purpose are often found through contribution to something larger than oneself.
Learning to tolerate uncertainty is a valuable skill in a rapidly changing world.
Supportive friendships can protect young people during periods of stress and transition.
Self-worth that depends entirely on achievement tends to be fragile and easily threatened.
Mental health literacy helps people recognise when they or others may need professional support.
Altruism raises fascinating questions about why humans sometimes act against their own immediate interests.
Forgiveness does not require forgetting harm, but it can release the burden of ongoing resentment.
Open conversations about wellbeing in schools help normalise help-seeking behaviour.
Ultimately, emotional strength often lies not in hiding feelings but in understanding and expressing them wisely.
p: Research in positive psychology suggests that wellbeing depends on more than the absence of illness. Factors such as positive emotions, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment all contribute to a flourishing life. While individual strategies such as gratitude journaling and exercise can help, social conditions also matter greatly. Secure housing, fair treatment and access to services provide the foundations upon which personal wellbeing can be built.

Perfectionism is increasingly common among young people, particularly high achievers. Although it can drive hard work, perfectionism is often associated with anxiety, procrastination and burnout, as individuals fear that anything less than flawless performance means failure. Psychologists distinguish between striving for excellence, which can be healthy, and the rigid belief that one's worth depends on achievement. Learning to accept mistakes as part of growth is a key step towards a healthier mindset.

Loneliness is not simply about being alone; it is the painful feeling that one's social connections are inadequate. Studies have linked chronic loneliness to poorer physical and mental health, with some researchers comparing its effects to well-known health risks. Young adults report high levels of loneliness despite being digitally connected. Community programs, shared interests and simple acts such as checking in with others can help rebuild a sense of belonging.

The stigma attached to mental illness remains one of the greatest barriers to recovery. People may fear being judged as weak, unreliable or dangerous, leading them to hide symptoms and delay treatment. Public campaigns, open discussion by well-known figures and mental health education in schools have helped reduce stigma in recent years. Nevertheless, attitudes towards some conditions, such as psychosis, remain more negative and require continued effort to change.

Restorative approaches to conflict, increasingly used in schools and justice systems, focus on repairing harm rather than simply assigning punishment. Participants discuss what happened, who was affected and how the harm can be addressed. This process encourages accountability and empathy, and it gives those who were harmed a voice. Advocates argue that restorative practices reduce repeat incidents, though they require skilled facilitation and genuine willingness from all parties.

Emotional intelligence, the capacity to recognise and manage one's own emotions and to understand those of others, is increasingly valued in education and the workplace. People with strong emotional intelligence tend to communicate effectively, resolve conflicts constructively and adapt well to change. Although some aspects may come naturally, these skills can be developed through reflection, feedback and practice. In a complex and interconnected world, they are as important as technical knowledge.
